Security Auditor should review: (1) VlcExecutablePath comes from user-controlled appsettings, fed directly to ProcessStartInfo.FileName — path traversal and arbitrary binary execution risk; (2) filePath comes from application data (movie catalog), also user-controlled. summary: Reviewed 4 files (IExternalPlayerService.cs, DesktopExternalPlayerService.cs, Program.cs, DesktopExternalPlayerServiceTests.cs). 0 Critical, 0 High findings. Security sign-off: PASS. The primary security surface is the process-launch path in DesktopExternalPlayerService — it correctly uses ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList with UseShellExecute=false, which fully mitigates shell/argument injection for filePath. The VlcExecutablePath-as-FileName trust model is inherent to user-configurable external tool paths in a local desktop application. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed; no blocking issues found. Three Low/Info observations recorded.

comments.note: A03 — Injection (MITIGATED): DesktopExternalPlayerService.BuildPlayStartInfo and BuildPlayFullscreenStartInfo (lines 67–83) use ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList.Add(filePath) with UseShellExecute=false. Arguments are passed directly to the OS as tokens — no shell expansion occurs. This correctly prevents command/shell injection regardless of filePath content. Pattern is safe and consistent with FfmpegRunner.

A03 — Injection (INFO): VlcExecutablePath from user settings is set as ProcessStartInfo.FileName (line 92). In a local desktop application, the user controlling appsettings.json is the same OS user running the process. Changing the VLC path to a different executable requires write access to the settings file, which is equivalent to existing local user access. No privilege escalation vector exists. This is by design for a configurable external-tool launcher — no remediation required.

A04 — Insecure Design (INFO): CreateBasePsi() at line 89 applies the null-forgiving operator (!) to VlcExecutablePath. This is safe because all callers (Play, PlayFullscreen) guard behind CanUseExternalPlayer, which already validates !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(VlcExecutablePath). The null-forgiving operator cannot be reached with a null value in production flow. The internal build helpers are accessible only to tests via InternalsVisibleTo — no public API exposure risk.

A04 — Insecure Design (INFO): filePath passed to Play/PlayFullscreen is not validated before launch (no existence check, no extension whitelist). This is acceptable for a local desktop player launcher — VLC handles missing or unplayable files gracefully. The path goes to VLC as an argument, not to a shell or interpreter, so there is no command execution risk from a malformed path.

summary: Reviewed 4 files: IExternalPlayerService.cs, DesktopExternalPlayerService.cs, Program.cs, DesktopExternalPlayerServiceTests.cs. No blocking issues found. All 6 ACs confirmed met. Interface design is minimal and focused. Implementation follows established project patterns (ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList, internal builder helpers for testability, early return vs throw on best-effort UI operations). CreateBasePsi() correctly omits RedirectStandard* and CreateNoWindow since VLC must open with a visible window. Null-forgiving operator usage is safe (callers always guarded by CanUseExternalPlayer). --fullscreen is correctly ordered before filePath in the argument list. DI registration is correct. Minor coverage gap: no test for CanUseExternalPlayer when UseVlc=true but VlcExecutablePath is empty — only one of the two conditions is exercised.

comments.note: DesktopExternalPlayerService.CreateBasePsi() correctly omits UseShellExecute, RedirectStandardOutput/Error, and CreateNoWindow flags. VLC is a windowed media player — suppressing its window or capturing its output would break the user experience. This is the correct design choice for an external player launcher, and intentionally differs from the FfmpegRunner pattern.

Play() and PlayFullscreen() return silently when CanUseExternalPlayer is false (with a LogWarning). Throwing an exception would be inappropriate here — the caller is a UI-triggered action and best-effort behavior is correct. The warning in the log gives visibility without crashing the application.

DesktopExternalPlayerServiceTests: CanUseExternalPlayer has one test (UseVlc=false returns false), but no test for the second condition: UseVlc=true && VlcExecutablePath null/empty should also return false. Low priority since the implementation is a simple && guard, but worth adding for completeness.
